essential: Paris, late 1903: Europe's silence (banks, press, embassies, Grand Dukes at the Ritz) while the East prepares for war; Adams cannot tell how much of Russian ignorance is real and how much is comedy. Frame this as his new problem of Russian inertia.

Return to Washington, January 1904: the country thinks as a world-power for the first time. Cassini's 'transparent blague' about the Japanese is read as an empty hand. Keep at least one quoted Cassini line.

White House supper as proxy for Brooks: Roosevelt's indiscreet candor, his claim that war could be stopped, and his reasons for restraint. Adams values the vigor of view more than the assertion of power.
Japan's force is methodical, not inert; Adams calls the war a 'Grammar of new Science' comparable to Pearson.
Hay's invisible diplomatic victory over Cassini; his reliance on Japan and England; Adams's hope for a quick peace after Port Arthur; Hay's declining strength set against a growing war.

St. Louis trip: smoke and cinders from Pittsburgh west, a new mixed population made by steam, and the Exposition's beautiful, empty electric illumination enjoyed 'with iniquitous rapture.' The hope is hedged as an optimist's, met by a conspiracy of silence in the East. Keep the line about urging Mrs. Roosevelt as the first and last.
Coutances and the Fete Dieu: the Virgin's 'Exposition' of about 1250 against the Senate closing St. Louis on Sunday. The Virgin's force is real enough to close fairs.

Buying the automobile, the force he most abominated, to study the Virgin as motive power; attraction as precise as a Newtonian formula; the Virgin as mistress who sees no difference in her lovers' ages.
The glass hunt from the 13th to the 16th century: the comic fragmentary window, the Beauvais and Chartres Trees of Jesse, and the question whether this is progress or a move toward multiplicity.
Troyes: news of Plehve's assassination; refuge in St. Pantaleon; the Ara Coeli question; which was he, murderer or murdered.
The Virgin never more One than in this failure; refusal to give up; the need to invent one's own formula. One seeks a spool, not absolute truth.
Resolution to write the Dynamic Theory of History in his garret.

essential: Definitions: progress, force, and man as a force; the theory admits it begs the question.
The inversion that forces capture man; the spider-in-web image with its fatal mistakes; man's early teachers (fire, water, animals, grains).
Man worships the whole as unity and God, even while blundering in choosing particular forces; religion as cultivation of occult force; hunger for infinite power as motive.
Antiquity progressed by economies, not new force (mathematics, Civil Law, coinage, roads); the means of motion stayed old.

The scandal of Rome's fall around 305 at the height of success, where Adams broke down on the steps of Ara Coeli. He rejects mineral exhaustion and argues the empire generated too much energy, too fast.

Unity on earth forced unity in heaven: Constantine's 'trust' (keep the Edict quotation as an 'Act of Congress'); In hoc signo vinces; Theodosius against Eugene as a boxing-match; the Cross as fetish-power like X-rays.
Slave and fetish as Rome's only engines; the vicious circle; Alaric in 410; Augustine's defence of spiritual over mechanical value, with his quotation.
The Middle Ages as a long experiment on occult force, producing architecture and art; Byzantium shows more varied forces.
The sudden arrival of the compass (which educated) and of Greek fire and gunpowder (diabolic educators), with St. Louis kneeling at Greek fire.

Even the innovators thought they served the Cross (Gutenberg, Columbus, Luther, the Puritans; the Church condemning anarchists, not atheists). Scientists doubted only the personality of Unity, never Unity itself.

Bacon reverses thought and force (keep at least one Bacon maxim). Acceleration after 1500 is involuntary; resistance is constant; a few score conductors like Franklin; then Newton, Franklin and Watt as men to whom forces 'stuck.'

New force is not in itself good; supersensual forces in 1900; the formula is admitted to be the oldest theory, with religion, philosophy and science diverging only at the edge (chaos or unity). It is a chart of convenience and needs a formula of acceleration.

The Priestley/Jenner/Fulton complaints are cuttable.

title: A DYNAMIC THEORY OF HISTORY (1904)

verbatim.purpose: Self-undercutting definition that founds the theory.
verbatim.text: A DYNAMIC theory, like most theories, begins by begging the question: it defines Progress as the development and economy of Forces.

verbatim.purpose: Central inversion: nature captures man.
verbatim.text: The sum of force attracts; the feeble atom or molecule called man is attracted; he suffers education or growth; he is the sum of the forces that attract him;

verbatim.purpose: Aphoristic triad, the theory's ethic of education.
verbatim.text: Susceptibility to the highest forces is the highest genius; selection between them is the highest science; their mass is the highest educator.

verbatim.purpose: Signature comic-commercial reading of the Edict of Milan.
verbatim.text: Good taste forbids saying that Constantine the Great speculated as audaciously as a modern stock-broker on values of which he knew at the utmost only the volume;

verbatim.purpose: Concrete deflation of religion as fetish-power.
verbatim.text: The laity, the people, the million, almost to a man, bet on the gods as they bet on a horse.

verbatim.purpose: Thesis linking the medieval and modern sections.
verbatim.text: This persistence of thought-inertia is the leading idea of modern history.

verbatim.purpose: The Baconian reversal stated as law.
verbatim.text: thought did not evolve nature, but nature evolved thought.

verbatim.purpose: Analogy that ties 1900 to the year 300; it closes the historical sweep.
verbatim.text: before which the man of science stood at first as bewildered and helpless as, in the fourth century, a priest of Isis before the Cross of Christ.

essential: The image of a new mass introduced on earth, accelerating toward a new equilibrium; the comet of 1843 that falls into the sun and returns, standing for the mind.

Measure by mass and attraction; society agrees to measure progress by coal. Coal doubles every ten years, with the ocean steamer as check: 30,000 horse-power in 1905 halved back to 234 for 1835. Intensity is hard to measure; radiation reveals a new universe; the ten-year ratio is conservative.

Carrying the series back: the ratio holds to 1820, after which mathematicians must help. Assume periods for the 18th and 17th centuries, then back to 1400; use the formula of squares for convenience. Before 1400 progress is slight but not stopped; medieval breaks are only apparent; the arrowhead is as convincing as the steam-engine.
Turgot and Comte affirmed the unity of progress; coal gives values; supersensual forces make calculation pressing.
The law will not relax for man's convenience; inertia ends in tragedy.

Science's 'stationary period' faith (Mill) is broken only by radium; nothing so revolutionary since 300; forces grip man like a live wire; the timid Paris gentleman and bombs doubling every ten years.
Before he was six he saw four impossibilities (steamer, railway, telegraph, Daguerreotype); the growing number of minds pursuing force; accidents and carnage; inexhaustible reservoirs.
Scientists caught between anarchy and order; the Pearson implication; the mind as comet, explosive, vegetable or saurian; an average mind failed by 1850.
The historian's docility toward the new American, 'a sort of God,' who may sit with Gibbon in 1964.

Folly of 1800 educating 1900; the teacher can only teach reaction; the quoted phrases from science textbooks; thinking in contradictions; the seventh doubling; movement from unity (1200) to multiplicity (1900); the mind must jump.

essential: Return to New York, November 5, 1904, nearly forty years after landing with his father and Motley; the city as hysteria; the demand for a new type of man; Fifth Avenue seen as Rome under Diocletian.
Washington: Roosevelt battling the Trusts; Adams's sympathy as a measure of motion; himself as an early victim who learned submission; whether the conflict will produce the new man.
Adams as impartial umpire: the Trusts are organized, Roosevelt's forces vague; the problem is to create a society able to manage the Trusts; man or nature, mind or motion.
His theory will verify itself within thirty years (the meteor near perihelion), so silence is wisest. The stance is admitted to be unmoral, yet it economizes waste of mind.
Nature's sympathy for death: Scott's seals (keep a short quotation) and Purun Dass; the Indian Summer of life should never be hustled.
Hay must rest; Mrs. Hay's plan; Adams's hope that Hay would make peace; Russia waits until her navy is destroyed, and the delay measures Hay's remaining time.

Hay revives on the voyage, recalling his first arrival at the Markoe house; the farewell with a smile; Adams reminds him of his achievements (the Atlantic system, a Roman pax in sight). Treaties are 'like lambs in a butcher's shop.'
Nervi, Nauheim, Paris; the decline; the final exchange.
'The rest is silence'; Hay's death learned at Armenonville; Adams is satisfied for Hay's sake; it was the summons to follow, not the shock; the three friends, and a return in 1938.
